extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent applicants drafting/examining applications in textile, architectural design, and computer-related inventions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examination and drafting of patent applications in textile, architectural design, and computer-related inventions, covering description requirements, claim construction, subject-matter eligibility, novelty/inventive_step, enablement, and evidence expectations. Useful for determining clarity, scope, and patentability across these technical fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of difference for fiber inventions specified by manufacturing method
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention specified by a spinning method proves its difference with the prior art through an example and a comparative example considering technical characteristics which assign a suitable property of matter to undrawn fiber formed immediately after spinning by heat treatment and drawing, the invention may be considered to be novel and to involve inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete examples and comparative examples that consider the technical characteristics (properties) imparted by the method to the product immediately after processing; such empirical comparisons can support novelty and inventive step for method-specified fiber claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction breadth for method-specified fiber materials
rubrics_metrics.description: In construing a claim relating to fiber material specified with a spinning method, the claim should not be construed to be limited by an embodiment presented in the description but should be construed to include a whole span of property of fiber material which is possible to produce according to the method specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claims to cover the full range of properties producible by the claimed method rather than being restricted to specific embodiments shown in the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textile inventions with additional design feature: subjective evaluation vs technical function
rubrics_metrics.description: Textile invention with additional design feature is evaluated subjectively since it has only characteristic of exterior beauty revealed by a textile structure or a processing method. If the structure or method is obvious or described in prior art, the invention lacks inventive step. However, if the structure of the design has new technical function, patentability can be recognized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish purely aesthetic (subjective) design effects from structural/process features that confer new technical function; only the latter support inventive step. If design effect arises merely from known structure/process, expect lack of inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of effect from minute/limited shape changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Minute different shape of a component (e.g., ring, traveler, metallic card clothing, knitting needle) may greatly influence the result; it is necessary to consider the effect from any difference between the shapes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When small shape differences are claimed, assess their technical effect. If effect is doubtful or difficult to be sure of, require test data or certified test results to establish the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination of textile inventions related to traditional art requires non-patent literature
rubrics_metrics.description: An application for traditional art (industrialization of traditional knowledge passed down) may be difficult to examine precisely only by searching patent documents; it is necessary to search non-patent documents and compare technical characteristics of the improved method with prior art of the field to determine inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include searches of non-patent literature (guides, manuals, traditional sources) when examining traditional textile arts (e.g., natural dyeing); compare improvements against traditional knowledge to assess inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expand prior-art scope for textile machinery to general machinery fields
rubrics_metrics.description: When examining inventive step of textile machinery, expand the scope of prior art search to general machinery fields not limited to related IPC D section, because textile industry has been developed with machine engineering since the Industrial Revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search broadly across general machine engineering and related technical fields; consider non-patent documents (device guidelines, catalogs) and well-known prior art in other technical fields when assessing obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider interdisciplinary technical fields where relevant (textile examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the skilled person in the textile field would reasonably consider other technical fields (e.g., PTFE/polyimide compounds, manufacturing epoxy resin having imide ring), those fields must be considered when assessing inventive step and obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete examples to identify cross-field prior art; examiners should consider chemistry or other relevant disciplines when the claimed textile solution utilizes materials or processes from those fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: State function of spaces in architectural design claims and description
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention on architectural design is made by combining space(s) with function(s). It is necessary to state function of the space in claim(s) and the description of the invention, and where it is not easy to recognize the functional effect from only the function of the space, interaction among functions of unit spaces should be additionally stated in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims and specifications for architectural designs must clearly identify the functions of unit spaces; when function alone isn't sufficient to show the invention, describe interactions among unit-space functions to complete the disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: When claiming shape/structure also disclose functions and interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: In architectural design, inventions can be stated by directly stating shape and structure (specifying the space) or by combination of interactive elements of spaces. Where shape and structure are directly stated, function of space and interaction among the functions should also be stated in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't rely solely on drawings or morphological descriptions; include functional explanations and interaction details in the specification even when the claim is structural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify category of claimed architectural invention (product vs method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must clearly specify whether the invention is directed to a product (e.g., an apartment), a method for constructing an apartment, or a method for designing an apartment, because unclear category leads to ambiguous subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to explicitly reflect the intended statutory category of protection; avoid language that mixes product and method unintentionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider public distribution timing of design documents for disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Design documents (drawings, specifications, calculation sheets) prepared for construction may be accessible to general persons; submission to public office for permission does not automatically mean public disclosure, but documents that are open in principle (e.g., official gazette for city plan) are considered distributed when accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether documents were actually accessible to the public when determining novelty/anticipation; filing with public offices does not equal public disclosure unless accessibility criteria are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural design subject-matter eligibility requires functions/interactions tied to products
rubrics_metrics.description: Invention of architectural design corresponds to product and method; unique characteristics include specification by division/combination of space and effects made by interaction among functions given to the space. Therefore, unless function is clearly recognized by unit space or products forming unit space, the function should be specified and interactions detailed to complete the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must relate the functional concept to concrete products/structures; functions alone are not the invention — claim a product that has the functions and interactions needed to realize the technical concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction for novelty/inventive step must include function (architectural)
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine inventive step of an architectural design invention, it is not allowed to construe claims by excluding the function; one must consider the function of the invention and its effect based on the function of space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid construing structural claims purely as placement/combination of spaces without their claimed functions; excluding functions can render claims unreasonably broad and anticipate by structurally-similar prior art with different purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible claim categories for computer-related inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A computer-related invention can be claimed as (1) a method by specifying a series of steps, (2) a product by specifying multiple functions performed thereby, (3) a computer-readable-program-recording medium having program code recorded thereon to install/execute/distribute the program, (4) a computer-readable medium having data recorded thereon when the data structure determines operations, and (5) a computer program recorded in a medium combined with hardware to accomplish a specific task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must be drafted to fall into statutory categories; claims to 'computer program not recorded in a medium' (a program per se) are not allowed. Use concrete language such as 'program recorded on a medium' or 'program makes the computer operate as ...' to avoid indefiniteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguous claim language like 'using a computer' (indefiniteness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions such as 'using a computer, comprising the steps of' can be indefinite because they permit multiple constructions (e.g., human-operated steps using a computer tool vs. an information-processing method by software).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify who/what performs each step (human vs computer/software) or rephrase to clearly indicate that the steps are performed by a computer program or by a human operating a computer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program vs functional means clarity in medium claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A program per se does not function as a 'means'. Claims should state that the program 'makes the computer operate as' the functional means rather than treating the program itself as the means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to attribute functions to the computer when run with the program (e.g., 'program recorded on a medium, the program makes the computer operate as X'), which yields definite claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define uncommon technical terms; undefined terms cause indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: If a term (e.g., 'the right-brain inference rule') is not defined in the description nor part of common general knowledge as of the filing, the claimed invention is unclear and indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide definitions or sufficient description for uncommon technical terms, abbreviations, symbols, etc., so the skilled person can understand the technical meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify technical relationships among claim elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely state elements (e.g., 'an information transmission medium transmitting a certain computer program') without showing technical relationships between elements cannot technically define a product invention and are unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include how elements interact or are arranged technically (structure, timing, causation) so that the claimed combination constitutes a technical invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify category for program signals/output/product distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Categories such as program signals, program signal sequence, program product, and program output must be clearly identified to determine the category of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague labels; explicitly claim as product/method/medium and describe how the claimed subject matter fits the statutory category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague scope-limiting terms (e.g., 'high speed')
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of comparative or qualitative terms like 'high speed' without objective comparison criteria makes the scope of the claimed invention unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either remove vague qualifiers or quantify them (e.g., specific throughput, latency) or rephrase to describe structural/functional features that yield the claimed performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims reciting only results without means are unclear
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim reciting only a result to be accomplished (e.g., a computer to predict down-burst) without concrete processing contents or means may be indefinite; unless the skilled person can introduce specific matter from the claim statement and common general knowledge, the scope is unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where function-only claims are used, ensure that either the skilled person can implement the function from the claim and common general knowledge, or include concrete means/procedures in the claim or description to make the invention definite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for when function-defined claims are acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine clarity of function-defined claims as follows: (①) if a person skilled in the art may introduce specific matter(s) with the function based on general knowledge, the scope is clear; (②) if not, scope is generally unclear; (③) exceptions where specification/drawings properly define the invention only by function or connection between function and level of technology is easily understood, scope may be clear; (④)-(⑤) special notes about parameter/manufacture-method claims and when novelty/infringement assessment becomes difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these tests when assessing functional claims; if the function cannot be linked to concrete embodiments or common knowledge, require amendment/clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement for computer-related inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must be such that a person skilled in the art, using ordinary technical means and ordinary creative activity, can carry out the claimed invention on the basis of the description, drawings, and common general knowledge as of the filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure sufficient disclosure of how to implement the invention in hardware/software terms; lack of implementation details may trigger rejection under enablement grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of enablement violations (abstract functional statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations include: (1) use of uncommon terms without definition; (2) abstract statements of steps/functions without disclosure on implementation so claimed invention cannot be carried out (e.g., business methods or game rules without computer implementation details; GUI steps without implementation); (3) hardware/software explained only by functional block diagrams or general flow charts insufficient to understand structure; (4) functional claims with embodiments explained only by flowcharts where relationship is unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete implementation details (algorithms, structure, modules, program listings with explanations) showing how functions are realized in hardware/software to meet enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notes on examiner action for insufficient disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: When the description is functional/operational, examiners must assess whether the disclosure is sufficiently clear and complete; if not, the examiner should notify the ground for rejection under the Patent Act 42(3)(i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should issue clear rejections and applicants should amend descriptions to supply concrete implementations or definitions; program listings may be included with sufficient explanation but cannot be used to amend the specification via external references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability assessment applies to claimed invention as defined by claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentability requirements are applied to 'claimed inventions' and the claimed invention is defined on the basis of claim language, interpreted in light of the specification, drawings, and common general knowledge as of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are the primary basis for patentability evaluation; carefully interpret claim terms in context of the specification when assessing novelty, inventive step and eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter eligibility for computer-related inventions: concrete implementation with hardware
rubrics_metrics.description: To be statutory subject matter, the claimed invention shall be 'a creation of technical ideas utilizing a law of nature.' Where information processing by software is concretely implemented by using hardware resources (software and hardware cooperatively working to implement arithmetic operation or manipulation of information depending on the use purpose), the apparatus/method/medium/program can be said to be qualified as a creation of technical ideas utilizing a law of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show cooperative working of software and hardware forming an apparatus/operational method particularly suitable for the use purpose. Merely describing information processing at an abstract level or showing input-processing-output flow without concrete hardware-software cooperation may be insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for assessing subject-matter eligibility (computer-related)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step (1) Understand the claimed invention based on claim language. (2) If information processing by software is concretely implemented by using hardware in the claimed invention (i.e., software and hardware cooperatively working to implement operations depending on use), the claimed invention constitutes statutory subject matter. (3) If not concretely implemented by hardware, it does not constitute statutory subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this three-step test when evaluating computer-related claims. Example: a computer that 'prepares a summary' may be non-statutory if the processing means are not shown to be cooperatively implemented with hardware.
